text: Taeo reached Haeseong after three hours, still unsure how to tell his family everything. Nib spotted the sea gate. It never closed, Taeo said. Nib asked who kept watch on it.
Grandpa waited at the stop with a cart of cardboard. Beyond him, fishing boats sat idle beneath a gate zone warning. Nib stepped off first, and Grandpa welcomed him with a courteous nod.
Taeo told Grandpa he didn't have to collect cardboard anymore. Grandpa said it was fine; the scrap yard was on the way. As they walked, Nib quietly steadied the stack.
Nib asked why the boats were asleep. Grandpa explained that the fish were inside the gate buoys, where nobody was allowed to go. The closed fishery sheds lined the road behind them.

Sixty-four kilos at fifty won a kilo earned Grandpa 3,200 won. Nib compared his twenty thousand for scouting. Grandpa advised him against cardboard. Taeo sent money every month, yet Grandpa still pulled the cart.
Haru burst out to meet them while Grandma shouted that she had said noon. Taeo apologised. Haru stopped in front of Nib, delighted to discover that the goblin was shorter than he was.

Nib pointed out that Haru was younger. Haru launched into dinosaur questions, ending with who would win against a T. rex. Nib answered that whoever saw the enemy first won. Haru objected. Nib stood by it.
Haru was glad Taeo had actually come, though he reminded him of his previous promise. The spicy seaweed snacks settled the argument. Taeo had remembered, and Haru decided he could stay.
Grandma welcomed Nib with an order to eat. Nib wiped his bare feet at the threshold. Taeo thanked Grandma for the bus fares. She said he would otherwise have walked.
Lunch was grilled mackerel from Norway. Grandma had sold fish from their own harbour for forty years. Nib took the seat facing the entrance and began neatly separating his fish with his fingers.
Removing the bones in one piece earned Grandma's approval. Then Nib noticed everyone else's chopsticks and tried using them.
Nib gripped one chopstick in each fist. Haru said he was holding them like knives. Nib judged them bad knives. Grandma let him use his hands. Grandpa and Haru joined him, earning a scolding.
Grandma demanded the story. Taeo explained that a gate had opened in the shop on Tuesday. Everyone had escaped. He had awakened as a summoner with low output. Haru approved: Taeo could stay home.
Grandma remembered Tuesday's message. Taeo had only told them he had eaten. He pointed out that he had. Her use of his full name left him with nowhere to hide.
He admitted he had been scared, so he hadn't called. Grandma asked whether he was hurt. When he said it was fine, she immediately told him not to start with that.
She asked again about gates. Taeo said Nib scouted ahead and told him what was there. He stayed outside. Grandpa's gaze moved from his bowl to the old family photograph.

Then Taeo explained Kanghan's offer: five years studying Nib, for fifty million won. The table erupted. Grandma shouted the amount back. Haru wanted to know how many snacks it would buy. Nib kept eating and caught a falling chopstick.

Grandma asked whether Taeo had refused. Nib answered, 'Eventually.' Taeo explained that he had told Pyo Nib wasn't his to sell. Grandma silently placed the biggest remaining piece of fish on Nib's plate.
The danger remained. In twenty days, a panel would decide whether Nib was a person or a construct. If they chose construct, he could be sold as property.
Haru said Sue the T. rex had sold for eight million dollars. Nib asked whether she had been alive. She hadn't. Then Sue hadn't got a say, he observed.
Grandma delivered her ruling. Nib had boned a mackerel at her table. He was a person, and Taeo could tell the panel she said so. Grandpa assured everyone it would be fine.
After lunch, Grandpa took Nib to the breakwater. Grandma said he never took anyone there. He called it the wall. Nib inspected it and approved: it was a good wall.
Grandpa poured tea, drank first, and offered Nib the cup. Nib noticed. Grandpa explained that they had always drunk first on watch. No request had been necessary.
Nib realised Grandpa watched the sea gate. Grandpa's explanation was simple: somebody should.
He had spent three years as a coastal conscript, taking night watches two hours at a time until his relief arrived. The last hour had been worse than the cold. But somebody always came to take over.
Nib said his own relief would find his post empty. Asked who that was, he named Kett, the scout he had trained. He held the cup still between his hands.
Grandpa looked back out to sea. 'Then he'll know you didn't run.' Nib's jaw finally relaxed. He looked down into his tea, then out toward the water again.
At the stop, Taeo felt the last bus had come too early. Haru presented Nib with a dinosaur sticker matching the one on Taeo's shouting brick.
Nib accepted it formally, promising to keep it dry. He pressed it carefully onto his pouch. Haru saluted, pleased with the ceremony.
Grandma packed food for both visitors and told Taeo to call. Typing that he had eaten wouldn't count. He promised. Haru still clung to the hem of his jacket.
Grandpa pressed his 3,200 won into Taeo's hand. Taeo protested that he had earned it hauling cardboard. Grandpa closed Taeo's fingers over the money and said it was fine.
Nib climbed aboard first. As Taeo followed, Grandpa straightened his backpack strap and looked toward the sea. 'Your father went in first too, you know.' Taeo froze. He hadn't heard that before.
The coach doors closed before Taeo could answer. Grandpa kept his eyes on the sea, his reassuring smile gone. His last words were a whisper: 'Don't you ever.'
